summary.text: Front matter of the 2021 WHO guidance 'Leave no one behind: guidance for planning and implementing catch-up vaccination', including copyright and licensing details, table of contents, acknowledgements, abbreviations, glossary of key terms, and an executive overview. It outlines how continuous catch-up vaccination and special post-disruption catch-up efforts close immunity gaps, strengthen primary health care, and reduce reliance on costly mass campaigns.

blocks.content: Figure 1, 'Elements of a strong catch-up vaccination strategy'. A circle divided into five coloured segments around a central circle labelled 'Catch-up vaccination policy and schedule'. The segments, clockwise from the top right, are: vaccines and supplies for catch-up vaccination; health worker knowledge and practice; recording and reporting practices, information systems and tools; communications and community engagement to build support; and strategies for catch-up vaccination.

blocks.title: Principles of catch-up vaccination
Introduction
blocks.content:
• 
Everyone should fully benefit from vaccination by receiving recommended vaccines as soon as they 
are eligible, and those who arrive “late” should not be denied vaccination.  
• 
Most vaccines are safe and effective to administer with no upper age limit and while timely 
vaccination should always be the aim, it is almost always better to vaccinate late than never.  
There are a small number of vaccines for which upper age limits do apply for administration3, but 
for most vaccine-preventable diseases (VPDs), providing vaccines late will still result in protection 
against morbidity and mort

summary.text: Introduces Section 1 on the core principles of catch-up vaccination, emphasizing that almost all vaccines are safe and effective to administer late when doses are missed and that no eligible individual should be denied vaccination. It highlights integrating catch-up vaccination into routine immunization programmes across all health system touchpoints to reduce missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV) and summarizes the elements of a strong catch-up strategy in Figure 1.

blocks.title: Establishing a catch-up vaccination policy and schedule
blocks.content:
• 
Every country should have a clear catch-up vaccination policy and catch-up schedule designed in 
line with the national immunization schedule. The catch-up policy should provide clarity to health 
workers on:  
1) The importance of providing vaccinations for those who have missed one or more doses 
within the national immunization schedule,  
2) How to determine eligibility including permissible age ranges,   
3) Correct recording and reporting of delayed doses, 
4) Leveraging every health contact as an opportunity to check vaccination history and catch 
up on vaccinations as appropriate.

summary.text: Outlines Section 1.1 on establishing a national catch-up vaccination policy and schedule aligned with the national immunization schedule, clarifying eligibility, permissible age ranges, recording of delayed doses, and screening at every health contact. It recommends engaging National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) and using the WHO recommendations for interrupted or delayed immunization summary tables to guide policy decision-making.

summary.text: Covers the remainder of Section 1.1 (including Box 1 on designing a catch-up schedule and policies for unconfirmed vaccination history) and Section 1.2 on ensuring the availability of vaccines and supplies for catch-up vaccination. It details forecasting additional buffer stock for older cohorts, applying the multi-dose vial policy (MDVP) to manage open-vial wastage, and using electronic stock management tools such as SMT, wVSSM, and eLMIS.

blocks.title: Building health worker knowledge and practice
blocks.content:
• 
The success of any health intervention depends on competent front-line health workers and 
managers. For catch-up vaccination to be viewed as a priority, health workers’ interpersonal skills, 
motivations and attitudes need to be addressed in training, supervision, and the feedback they are 
given. For programmes that historically limited routine immunization to children <1 year, or 
children <2 years, the expansion of catch-up to older age groups may be entirely new to health 
workers and require a shift in both attitude and practice.

summary.text: Presents Section 1.3 on building health worker knowledge, attitudes, and practices for administering catch-up vaccinations across expanded age groups through training, supportive supervision, and clear job aids. It includes Box 2, an 11-step summary of operational instructions for health workers covering vaccination history review, minimum ages and intervals, co-administration of multiple overdue antigens, recording actual dose numbers, and scheduling follow-up visits.

blocks.title: Recording and reporting of catch-up vaccination doses
blocks.content:
• 
A major challenge for identifying eligibility, administering and monitoring catch-up vaccination is 
lack of reliable written record of vaccination history (i.e. individual home-based records, facility-
based paper registers, or EIRs). 
• 
Many immunization information systems are not currently designed to record, and report delayed 
doses. For example, administrative systems typically record vaccinations by yearly age range (e.g. 0-
11m, 12-23m, etc.) or only for the exact age of eligibility (e.g. HPV at 10 years). However, these 
restrictive formats may lead to unintended consequences, su

summary.text: Addresses Section 1.4 on recording and reporting catch-up vaccination doses, explaining how restrictive age-grouped tally sheets, registers, and 12-month coverage reporting cycles can inadvertently discourage late vaccination. It provides guidance on redesigning paper registers, tally sheets, and electronic immunization registries (EIRs) to capture delayed doses, discusses denominator challenges in Box 3, and outlines solutions for strengthening home-based records (HBRs) in Box 4.

blocks.title: Communication and community engagement
blocks.content:
• 
Targeted communications should inform individuals, caregivers, and communities more broadly of 
the value of vaccination and the importance of being vaccinated in a timely manner. 
• 
Communication with caregivers and individuals through phone calls, emails, and SMS text message 
reminders, as well as broader messaging through television, radio, social media, posters, etc. should 
aim to increase awareness that missing a scheduled vaccination does not necessarily mean that 
individuals are no longer eligible: vaccines given late are still safe and effective at providing 
protection against

summary.text: Covers Section 1.5 on communication and community engagement for ongoing catch-up vaccination, emphasizing targeted reminders and broad media messaging that late vaccination remains safe and effective. It highlights partnering with civil society, faith-based groups, daycares, and schools to reach vulnerable populations, counter misinformation, and encourage caregivers to bring home-based records to every health visit.

blocks.title: Strategies for catch-up vaccination
blocks.content:
Routine immunization services throughout the year 
• 
The practice of catch-up vaccination should be integrated into routine immunization service 
delivery on a continuous basis.  Every immunization contact, whether fixed or outreach (including 
school-based), should be used as an opportunity to review an individual’s vaccination status and 
catch-up any antigens that have been missed before that visit. 
• 
Every health facility should have a process in place for newborn and defaulter tracking and for 
identifying and reaching zero-dose children in their catchment area (see Box 3). 
• 
Creativ

summary.text: Details Section 1.6 on operational strategies for continuous catch-up vaccination, including newborn and defaulter tracking in routine immunization, integrating 'screen and vaccinate' or referral workflows across broader health services to reduce missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV), and implementing school-based vaccination checks at educational enrollment or during sessions.

Immunization is an essential health service that should continue without interruption to the 
maximum extent possible under all circumstances. However, in exceptional emergency or disaster 
situations there may be an interruption or significant drop in routine immunization services, delay 
or temporary suspension of mass vaccination campaigns, and/or prolonged vaccine shortages, 
leading to an accumulation of individuals susceptible to one or more VPDs.

immunization service deli

summary.text: Introduces Section 2 on special catch-up vaccination efforts following an interruption of immunization services caused by emergencies, disasters, or vaccine shortages. It stresses integrating ongoing catch-up into routine services as soon as delivery resumes while planning large-scale, intensified efforts and cohort tracking when prolonged disruptions create substantial immunity gaps.

blocks.title: Policy and advocacy
blocks.content:
• 
During, or in the aftermath of a catastrophic event, whether it be an outbreak, epidemic or 
pandemic, natural disaster, acute conflict, or other disruption, health systems are likely to be 
overburdened.33 Finances and human resources may be limited due to reallocation. Supply chains 
may be disrupted leading to stock-outs of vaccines and supplies. Surveillance systems may have 
been stopped or diverted. There may be decreased demand for immunization services (due to 
misinformation, fear, inaccessibility, limitation in mobility, competing priorities, previous 
disruptions in services, etc

summary.text: Outlines Section 2.1 on policy and advocacy during and after catastrophic events or health system disruptions, calling for immunization recovery to be embedded within coordinated health system recovery plans. It recommends issuing interim catch-up guidance—such as temporarily lifting upper age limits for cohorts missed during disruptions—in consultation with NITAGs and emergency programmes, and rapidly disseminating updated schedules and job aids to all providers.

blocks.title: Managing vaccines and supplies
blocks.content:
• 
During an interruption in services, supply chains at local, regional, national, and possibly international 
levels may be affected. Stock out of key supplies may be a challenge, requiring a remapping of 
inventory, at all levels, and a coordinated redistribution of supplies once delivery channels are 
reopened.  
• 
The situation can be mitigated by the following actions: 
o Establish and implement procedures for safeguarding and maximizing in-country stocks of 
vaccines through robust management of temperature records, VVM indicators and expiry 
dates.  
o Account for any expired or damage

summary.text: Presents Section 2.2 on managing vaccines and supplies during and after service interruptions, including inventory remapping, temperature and VVM monitoring, forecasting surge stock for missed cohorts, and assessing cold chain capacity. It also covers accepting reduced shelf-life vaccines managed under the 'first expiry, first out' (FEFO) principle and utilizing Controlled Temperature Chain (CTC) or Extended Controlled Temperature Conditions (ECTC) where licensed.

blocks.title: Monitoring the extent of the interruption
blocks.content:
• 
It is important to monitor the situation as closely as possible throughout the period of disruption 
and track individuals or cohorts missing vaccination as best as possible to inform catch-up 
strategies.  This can be done by: 
o Continuing to monitor vaccination coverage, VPD surveillance, AEFIs, and vaccine safety 
concerns in order to identify gaps, inequalities and vulnerable groups and communities.  
o Maintaining a logbook of the population with pending vaccines, including newborns during 
the period of disruption, based on individual records (facility-based paper immunization 
regis

summary.text: Covers Section 2.3 on monitoring the extent of service interruptions by tracking coverage, VPD surveillance, AEFIs, and facility logbooks of individuals with pending doses, alongside Box 5 on estimating target populations for intensified catch-up efforts. It also recommends rapid coverage assessments, risk triangulation, and interim recording practices on home-based records and registers when formal information systems lack fields for delayed doses.

blocks.title: Communication and community engagement
blocks.content:
• 
Even if routine immunization services have continued at reduced capacity or once they resume, 
demand and accessibility may remain low and intermittent interruptions may continue to occur for 
some time.  
• 
Engagement with communities (including local civil society, non-governmental and faith-based 
organizations, professional associations, etc.) to help design and implement tailored and targeted 
communication strategies will be essential to restore and rebuild community confidence in vaccines 
and/or immunization services. 
• 
If possible, formative research should be conducted to learn

summary.text: Addresses Section 2.4 on communication and community engagement following service disruptions to rebuild public trust, counter rumours through media and digital listening, and conduct formative research on barriers to immunization. It emphasizes informing communities that individuals remain eligible for missed doses, that late vaccines are safe and effective, and where and when services are operating with safety precautions.

blocks.title: Strategies for catch-up vaccination after an interruption of services
blocks.content:
• 
Offering catch-up vaccination on an ongoing basis through the routine immunization system is the 
least resource intensive and most sustainable strategy for ensuring individuals are able to receive 
the vaccines they are due, especially if the service interruption is relatively short.  
• 
If immunization services have been impacted for a prolonged period of time, additional strategies 
to accelerate catch-up vaccination efforts will likely be needed, to reach larger groups and close 
immunization gaps as quickly as possible.   
• 
Depending on the extent and duration of the disruption in i

summary.text: Details Section 2.5 on selecting and combining strategies for catch-up vaccination after prolonged service interruptions, including intensified routine outreach, Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization (PIRI), and supplementary immunization activities (SIAs). It provides decision-making frameworks in Boxes 6 and 7 for epidemiological VPD risk assessment, vaccine delivery amenability, contextual constraints, and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures.

blocks.content: A table headed 'Minimum interval from the most recent dose administered'. Rows give the age-appropriate vaccine: 1-4 years, DTwP, DTaP or DT; 4-7 years, DTwP, DTaP, Td or DT; over 7 years, Td or TdaP. Columns give the dose, with the same interval for all three rows: 1st dose as early as possible; 2nd dose at least 4 weeks after the 1st; 3rd dose at least 6 months after the 2nd; 4th dose at least 1 year after the 3rd; 5th dose at least 1 year after the 4th.

blocks.title: Designing Catch-up Vaccination Schedules
blocks.content:
Every country should have a catch-up vaccination schedule designed in line with the national 
immunization schedule, that adhere to any upper or lower age requirements as determined by the 
national immunization policy. NITAGs should be involved in the process of developing a catch-up 
vaccination schedule at the earliest opportunity.  
Catch-up vaccination schedules can be designed in a variety of ways and, as immunization programmes 
and schedules vary considerably across countries (and sometimes within), it is not possible to 
recommend a ‘generic’ catch-up schedule.

summary.text: Presents Annex 1 on designing national, antigen-specific, and population-specific catch-up vaccination schedules with NITAG involvement, linking to country schedule examples. It includes Table A1.1 illustrating a tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) catch-up schedule and Table A1.2 summarizing WHO recommendations for interrupted or delayed routine immunization across antigens.

blocks.title: Minimum Intervals between Doses in a Vaccine Series
blocks.content:
For vaccines requiring multiple doses, the minimum interval is the shortest amount of time permissible between 
doses in order to provide an adequate immune response. If the interval between the doses is shorter than the 
minimum interval, the second dose received may not be effective. 
Refer to WHO recommendations for interrupted or delayed immunization to design an catch-up vaccination 
schedule and job aids to assist health workers in assessing eligibility for vaccination when an individual has missed 
or delayed doses.

blocks.content: An 'Instructions' panel of three steps for the health worker. Step 1: praise the parent or caregiver for bringing the child, and find out from the immunization record or caregiver how old the child is today and which vaccines the child has already received. Step 2: use the chart to the right to decide what to give; the child should already have received all vaccines due up to their current age, and if doses are missing it is not too late; administer the vaccines for which the child is eligible, respecting the necessary spacing. Step 3: remind the caregiver when to bring the child back for subsequent doses and emphasise the importance of completing the series. Cartoon drawings of a standing girl and a seated baby decorate the panel.

A chart titled 'Which vaccines can be given today?', with the line 'It is better to vaccinate late than never!'. Rows are ages (birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 9 months, 18 months, 2 years); coloured columns are vaccines, each starting at the age of its first dose and running downward as an arrow. HepB BD and BCG start at birth, HepB BD ending at a stop sign; OPV 1-3, PCV 1-3, Penta 1-3 and RV 1-3 at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, RV ending at a stop sign before 2 years; IPV at 14 weeks; MCV 1 at 9 months; DTP4 (or Penta4), MCV 2 and MenA at 18 months. A 'When to give' column gives the timing for each row (for example, at 10 weeks or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after dose 1), and a 'When not to give' column gives the limits: HepB BD not after 6 weeks; RV1, RV2 and RV3 not after 2 years of age; later doses not before 4 weeks since the previous dose; MCV1 and MenA not before 9 months of age except where indicated. A footer says there is no need to restart a series after a long gap, and there is no upper age limit for most vaccines except rotavirus (under 2 years) and the hepatitis B birth dose (under 6 weeks).

blocks.title: Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization: An Overview
blocks.content:
The note below was developed in October 2018 by an ad-hoc workgroup on PIRI.a 
About 
Periodic intensification of routine immunization (PIRI) is an umbrella term to describe a spectrum of 
time-limited, intermittent activities used to administer routine vaccinations to under-vaccinated 
populations and/or raise awareness of the benefits of vaccination.  Example activities include Child 
Health Days, Child Health Weeks, and National Vaccination Weeks (Table A6.1).  Historically, a PIRI 
that included delivery of vaccinations also included delivery of other key maternal and child health 
(MCH) i

summary.text: Presents Annex 6, an overview developed by the ad-hoc workgroup on Periodic Intensification of Routine Immunization (PIRI) describing time-limited, intermittent activities such as Child Health Days and Vaccination Weeks where doses are screened and recorded as routine immunizations. It includes Tables A6.1–A6.3 detailing PIRI goals, a feature comparison against SIAs and routine immunization, and potential PIRI designs tailored to country coverage settings.

blocks.title: Actions to enhance acceptance and demand for vaccination
blocks.content:
KEY POINTS 
• 
Vaccination uptake is affected by both individual, social and practical factors. This includes the 
convenience and experience of immunization services, as well as community trust in vaccines 
and local or national authorities. 
• 
Building acceptance and demand for vaccination not only contributes to closing immunity gaps 
but strengthens resilience in the face of vaccine-related events (e.g. outbreaks, AEFIs, rumours / 
misinformation), to minimise the negative impact of such events. 
• 
Intensified efforts are needed to support vaccine demand in the context of service disrupt

summary.text: Presents Annex 7 on actions to enhance acceptance and demand for vaccination, outlining key communication messages during and after service disruptions, collaboration with local civil society and community leaders, and rumour management. It also covers behavioural and social data collection, health worker training in interpersonal communication, and service quality improvements that foster positive vaccination experiences.
